extraction_text: Vidura narrates an ancient dialogue to illustrate a point.
Vidura cites a conversation between the sage Adharya (or Atri) and the Satya deities.

attributes.relationships: The Satya deities seek wisdom from the sage.

extraction_text: The Satya deities encounter a great sage who has taken the form of a swan and ask him to speak wise words.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Sage transforms into a swan; deities are divine beings.

extraction_text: The swan (sage) delivers teachings on righteous conduct, including non-violence, truthfulness, self-control, and avoiding harsh speech.
The swan explains that enduring harm transfers the attacker's merit to the victim and that one's character is influenced by their associations.
The swan classifies people into superior, middling, and inferior based on their virtues, actions, and associations.

key_points: Superior: wish happiness for all, truthful, self-controlled

extraction_text: The swan advises serving superior people, appropriately serving middling people, and avoiding inferior people to cultivate goodness.

attributes.relationships: Guidance on social conduct and self-improvement.

extraction_text: The swan concludes that while effort can bring wealth, true praise and noble character come from virtuous living, not merely acquisition.
Dhritarashtra responds, indicating he has heard Vidura's narration.

attributes.relationships: Dhritarashtra is the listener to Vidura's advice.

extraction_text: Dhritarashtra asks Vidura about the characteristics of noble families.

attributes.relationship: Dhritarashtra is a Kuru king, Vidura is his half-brother and minister.

extraction_text: Vidura lists the seven qualities of noble families: austerity, self-control, knowledge of Brahman, sacrifice, marital purity, regular food charity, and correct conduct.
Vidura further explains noble families have good conduct, pure birth, implement dharma through good deeds, desire family honor, and reject falsehood.

Vidura states families lose noble status by: not performing sacrifices, impure marriages, abandoning Vedas, violating dharma, wasting resources, seizing Brahmin property, offending Brahmins, suppressing/slandering Brahmins, or stealing from Brahmins.
Vidura emphasizes conduct over wealth - families with wealth but lacking conduct are not noble, while poor families with good conduct are noble and renowned.
Vidura expresses wishes for their family to avoid: those who make enemies, ministers who steal, those who harm friends, deceivers/liars, and those who eat before serving ancestors/gods/guests.
Vidura says those who kill Brahmins, hate Brahmins, or engage in farming should not approach their family.
Vidura describes what good households never lack: grass, land, water, and friendly speech.
Vidura compares noble-born people to the Shyandana tree that can bear burdens others cannot.
Vidura defines true friendship: not angry/fearful people, not those requiring careful service, but father-like trustworthy friends.
Vidura states non-relatives with friend-like qualities become relatives, friends, shelter, and support.
Vidura warns against fickle-mindedness, not serving elders, and uncontrolled senses which lead to losing wealth and friends.
Vidura criticizes those who get angry without cause and give favors arbitrarily like changing clouds.
Vidura condemns those who don't treat friends well or help them, saying even carnivores won't eat such ungrateful corpses.
Vidura advises asking friends for help regardless of wealth to test friendship.
Vidura explains how worries harm appearance, strength, wisdom, and cause disease while pleasing enemies.
Dhritarashtra expresses regret for wronging King Yudhishthira and fears his sons will be destroyed in battle.

attributes.relationship: Dhritarashtra wronged Yudhishthira; Yudhishthira is a threat to Dhritarashtra's sons

extraction_text: Dhritarashtra asks Vidura for words to dispel his agitation.
Vidura advises that peace comes only through knowledge, austerity, sense control, and renunciation of desire.
Vidura states that fear is dispelled by wisdom, greatness is sought through austerity, knowledge is gained from a teacher, and peace comes through renunciation.
Vidura describes the liberated one as free from desire and hatred, wandering without relying on charity or Vedic rituals.
Vidura advises to study well, fight well, act well, and practice austerity well for happiness to grow.
Vidura warns that divided people find no sleep, pleasure, praise, happiness, or respect; they are unfit for counsel or protecting property, with death as their only end.
Vidura states wealth comes from cows, austerity from Brahmins, chatter from women, and fear from relatives.
Vidura uses the metaphor of many threads twisted together to bear a heavy load, advising unity.

attributes.action: Metaphorical advice for strength through unity

extraction_text: Vidura compares relatives to coals: separated they only smoke, together they burn brightly.
Vidura warns that those who are violent toward Brahmins, women, relatives, and cows will fall like ripe fruit from a tree.

attributes.action: Warning against violence toward protected groups

extraction_text: Vidura uses the metaphor of a single tree being blown down by wind, while a forest stands firm, advising mutual support among relatives.

attributes.metaphor: Single tree vs. forest in a storm
attributes.lesson: Isolation makes one vulnerable; mutual support ensures prosperity

extraction_text: Vidura states one must not kill Brahmins, cows, women, children, and relatives, or eat their food, or fail to give them shelter.

attributes.action: Moral injunction against harm and duty of protection

extraction_text: Vidura states health is the greatest asset, as sickness is akin to death.
Vidura describes anger as a severe, non-physical headache connected to sin, urging Dhritarashtra to swallow his anger and be calm.
维杜罗劝告持国阻止难敌在掷骰子赌博中采用欺骗手段，并建议让俱卢族和般度之子们联合起来共同繁荣。

attributes.relationships: 维杜罗是持国的顾问，持国是俱卢族国王，难敌是持国之子，般度之子们是持国的侄子们

attributes.relationships: 持国向维杜罗请教寿命问题

extraction_text: A wise person who is generous, truthful, eats sacrificial leftovers, non-violent, avoids useless actions, avoids disputes, grateful, sincere, and gentle ascends to heaven.
Flatterers are easy to find, but those who speak and listen to harsh truths are rare.
A king who upholds righteousness and listens to unpleasant truths has a true friend.
Sacrifice one for family, family for village, village for country, and earth for self (soul).
Protect property to prevent disaster, use property to protect wife, and use both to protect self.
The speaker previously warned the king against gambling, but the king did not listen.
The Kauravas defeating the Pandavas is likened to crows defeating peacocks; the king is warned of future sorrow for abandoning the lion (Pandavas) and protecting jackals (Kauravas).

attributes.metaphor: Crows vs. Peacocks, Lion vs. Jackals

extraction_text: Servants trust a master who never gets angry; such servants remain loyal even in misfortune.
Do not reduce servants' livelihoods to compete with outsiders; even friendly ministers will abandon if deprived.
Consider tasks first, provide fair treatment, gain help, and accomplish difficult things.
A loyal servant understands the master's intent, works diligently, speaks for the master's benefit, and should be trusted.
A servant who is careless, defiant, arrogant, and quarrelsome should be dismissed quickly.
An envoy should have eight qualities: not arrogant, not humble, not procrastinating, compassionate, amiable, incorruptible, healthy, and noble in speech.
A wise person avoids entering others' homes confidently at wrong times, standing at crossroads at night, or pursuing royal women.
Avoid conflict with hypocrites; do not say 'I don't trust you' directly, but find a reasonable excuse.
Avoid entanglement with these: kind people, kings, prostitutes, royal servants, sons, brothers, orphans and widows, soldiers, and dishonored people.
Those who bathe regularly have ten features: strength, beauty, pure pronunciation, comfortable touch, elegant fragrance, cleanliness, auspiciousness, tenderness, and beautiful women.
The text describes six characteristics of a person who controls their diet: health, longevity, happiness, energy, good reproductive quality, and freedom from accusations of gluttony.

The text advises against allowing certain types of people to live in one's home: those with bad behavior, gluttony, who offend the public, are cunning, cruel, disheveled, and who act inappropriately regarding time and place.

The text advises against begging from certain people even in misfortune: misers, slanderers, the uneducated, the degenerate, those who blindly respect others, the rude and arrogant, those who hold grudges, and the ungrateful.
The text advises against serving six types of people: those with vile behavior, gossipers, habitual liars, the impious, the emotionally cold, and the arrogant.
The text states that purpose and means are interdependent; one cannot exist without the other.
The text describes the life stages: after having sons, repaying debts, arranging their livelihoods, and marrying off all daughters, a man can retire to the forest and live like a sage (Muni).
The text states that a ruler should work for the welfare of all beings, which also brings personal happiness, as this is the root of success in dharma and profit.
The text rhetorically asks how a person with wisdom, strength, radiance, courage, diligence, and perseverance could fear lacking a livelihood.

The speaker references the evil consequences of the quarrel with the sons of Pandu (Pandavas), which shocked even the gods including Indra (also called Sakra, standardized to Indra): sons become enemies, life becomes restless, reputation is destroyed, and enemies rejoice.

attributes.relationships: Indra is a god; Pandavas are the sons of Pandu.
attributes.supernatural_elements: Reference to gods (Indra and other deities) being shocked.

extraction_text: The speaker warns that the anger of Bhishma, you (the listener, likely Duryodhana or another Kaurava), Drona, and Yudhishthira (referred to as 'King Yudhishthira' or 'Dharma Raja', standardized to Yudhishthira) would destroy the world like a white comet falling from the sky.

attributes.relationships: Bhishma is a Kuru elder; Duryodhana is a Kaurava prince; Drona is a teacher; Yudhishthira is the eldest Pandava.
attributes.supernatural_elements: Comparison to a comet destroying the world.

extraction_text: The speaker states that Duryodhana's hundred sons, Karna, and the five Pandavas could rule the entire earth girdled by the seas.

attributes.relationships: Duryodhana's sons are Kauravas; Karna is an ally of the Kauravas; Pandavas are their cousins/enemies.

extraction_text: The speaker analogizes the Kauravas (sons of Dhritarashtra) as a forest and the Pandavas as tigers, advising not to cut down the forest with tigers or drive the tigers from the forest, as they are interdependent.

attributes.relationships: Kauravas and Pandavas are rival cousins in the Kuru dynasty.

extraction_text: The text states that a person with evil thoughts does not want to know their own faults or the virtues of others.
The text advises that to gain the highest profit, one must follow dharma from the beginning, as profit does not separate from dharma, just as nectar does not separate from heaven.
The text states that a soul that abandons evil and focuses on good can know everything, whether original or derived.
The text advises that by timely implementation of dharma, profit, and desire, one achieves their combination in this life and the next.
The text advises controlling impulses of anger and joy to enjoy good fortune and remain unconfused even in adversity.

The text describes five powers of a person: physical strength (smallest), gaining loyal ministers (second), winning wealth (third), inherited strength from father and grandfather (fourth, called innate strength), and intellect (best, as it enables gaining everything).
The text warns that if a person severely harms others, oppresses them, and makes enemies, they will not feel safe even at a distance.
A series of proverbial warnings and analogies are presented.

attributes.action: The speaker advises against trusting certain entities (women, kings, snakes, etc.) and warns not to underestimate others (snakes, fire, lions, noble offspring).

extraction_text: An analogy compares the listener and his son to a creeper vine and the Pandavas to Sal trees.

attributes.action: The speaker states the creeper (listener and son) cannot grow without clinging to a great tree (the Pandavas).
attributes.relationships: Implies the listener's side is dependent on the Pandavas.

extraction_text: A second analogy compares the listener and his son to a forest and the Pandavas to lions within it.

attributes.action: The speaker states a forest (listener's side) is destroyed without lions (Pandavas), and lions (Pandavas) are also destroyed without a forest (listener's side).
attributes.relationships: Describes a relationship of mutual dependence and potential mutual destruction between the two sides.

extraction_text: The text is identified as Chapter 37 of the Udyoga Parva (Book of Effort) in the Mahabharata.

attributes.action: Identifies the literary source and context of the preceding dialogue.
